parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Frailty: recognising and assessing it
blurb: Score the Clinical Frailty Scale on the right baseline and choose the NICE NG56 frailty tool that fits the setting.
question: Mrs Begum, 82, is admitted with pneumonia and today needs two staff to move in bed. Two weeks ago she washed and dressed herself but needed help with shopping, housework, all outside activities and bathing. The doctor asks the nurse to record her Clinical Frailty Scale score. Which score should be recorded?

teach.body: Frailty is a loss of the body's reserve, so that a small stress (a urine infection, a new tablet, a move to hospital) causes a large, sudden fall in function. NICE NG56 lists frailty as a 'symptom complex' that counts as a long-term condition in multimorbidity, and as one reason to offer an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity. Plain English: two people of 82 can look the same in a chair, but one bounces back from illness and the other does not. Recognising frailty early shapes every later decision.

teach.caption: Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale, version 2.0 (2020). Score it with clinical judgement.

head: Level
Key feature (paraphrased)
rows: Conditions controlled; not active beyond routine walking
Independent, but 'slowed up' or tired; symptoms limit
Help with finances, transport, heavy housework
Help with all outside activities, housework, bathing
Dependent for personal care, but stable
Dependent and approaching end of life
teach.caption: Level 9 is for people with a life expectancy under 6 months who are not otherwise living with severe frailty.

teach.body: The Clinical Frailty Scale describes how the person was BEFORE this illness: their usual state about two weeks before they became acutely unwell. Someone who is bedbound with pneumonia today may have been walking to the shops a fortnight ago. Ask the person, family or carers, and check records. In people with dementia, the degree of frailty generally corresponds to the degree of dementia: someone with moderate dementia who manages personal care with prompting usually sits around level 6.
teach.cite: Clinical Frailty Scale v2.0 guidance (Dalhousie University, 2020)

teach.text: Two classic errors: scoring how the person looks TODAY in an acute illness (it inflates the score), and doing a physical performance test such as Timed Up and Go while the person is acutely unwell. NICE NG56 says be cautious assessing frailty in someone acutely unwell, and do not use a physical performance tool.

teach.h: NICE NG56 frailty tools by setting

rows.label: Gait speed
values: Informal or formal (over 5 s for 4 m)

rows.label: Activity scale (PASE)
values: 56 or less men, 59 or less women

teach.caption: NG56 recs 1.4.4–1.4.5. Consider using one of these; eFI can flag people at risk from GP records (1.3.2).

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Begum on the medical ward
teach.body: Mrs Begum, 82, is admitted with pneumonia and needs two staff to move. Her daughter explains that two weeks ago she washed and dressed herself but needed help with shopping, housework, every trip outside and bathing. The nurse scores her CFS on that baseline: level 6, living with moderate frailty, not 7 or 8. She does not attempt a Timed Up and Go while Mrs Begum is acutely unwell, and records where the information came from.

children.label: Be cautious; no performance tests
children.sub: Score CFS on the baseline from history

children.label: Choose a tool for the setting
Outpatients
children.sub: Adds Timed Up and Go and PASE

items: Consider an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity (frailty or falls is a trigger).
Look for falls risk and offer a comprehensive falls assessment where in scope.
Review medicines: lower overall benefit of preventive treatments is likely with frailty.
Share the score and its source so later teams use the same baseline.
CFS v2.0 has 9 levels, from 1 Very fit to 9 Terminally ill.
Score the person's usual state about 2 weeks before the acute illness, using clinical judgement.
Level 5 needs help with finances, transport, heavy housework; level 6 with all outside activities and bathing; level 7 is dependent for personal care but stable.
NG56: TUG over 12 s, gait over 5 s for 4 m, PRISMA-7 of 3 or more, self-rated health 6 or less.
Do not use physical performance tools when someone is acutely unwell.

summary: You can now score the Clinical Frailty Scale on the person's baseline and tell the levels apart. You can also choose the right NICE NG56 frailty tool for the setting and know when not to use one.

A.q: Before his admission, Mr Hayes, 84, needed help with all outside activities and with keeping house. He had difficulty with stairs and needed help to bathe, but managed his own personal care. Which Clinical Frailty Scale level fits his baseline?
options: Level 5, living with mild frailty
Level 7, living with severe frailty
Level 4, living with very mild frailty
Level 6, living with moderate frailty
A.why: CFS v2.0 level 6: needs help with all outside activities and keeping house, often has problems with stairs, and needs help with bathing.

whyNot.0: Level 5 needs help with higher-order tasks such as finances, transport and heavy housework, not all outside activities and bathing.
whyNot.1: Level 7 is completely dependent for personal care; he managed his own.
whyNot.2: Level 4 is independent of daily help, with symptoms limiting activities.

A.q: A practice nurse uses a formal gait speed test with Mrs Lane, 79, who is well today. Under NICE NG56, which time to walk 4 metres indicates frailty?
options: More than 3 seconds
More than 5 seconds
More than 8 seconds
More than 12 seconds
A.why: NG56 recs 1.4.4–1.4.5: a formal gait speed assessment with more than 5 seconds to walk 4 metres indicates frailty.

whyNot.0: 3 seconds is not the NICE threshold; it is 5 seconds.
whyNot.2: 8 seconds is too long; frailty is indicated from more than 5 seconds.
whyNot.3: More than 12 seconds is the Timed Up and Go threshold, a different test.

A.q: Mr Ortiz, 70, has advanced cancer with a life expectancy of under 6 months. He still walks his dog daily and manages all his own care. Which Clinical Frailty Scale level describes him?
options: Level 9, terminally ill
Level 8, very severe frailty
Level 7, severe frailty
Level 3, managing well
A.why: CFS v2.0 level 9 applies to people approaching the end of life with a life expectancy under 6 months who are not otherwise living with severe frailty.

whyNot.1: Level 8 is completely dependent for personal care and approaching end of life; he is independent.
whyNot.2: Level 7 is completely dependent for personal care; he is not.
whyNot.3: Level 3 does not reflect a life expectancy under 6 months, which the scale places at level 9.

B.q: In a hospital outpatient clinic, Mr Price, 79, is well. His PRISMA-7 score is 2 and his Timed Up and Go time is 14 seconds. How should the nurse interpret these results?
options: Frailty is indicated by his PRISMA-7 score
No frailty, as his PRISMA-7 is below 3
Frailty is indicated by his Timed Up and Go time
Neither test is valid for use in hospital outpatient settings
B.why: NG56 rec 1.4.5: in outpatients, a Timed Up and Go time of more than 12 seconds indicates frailty. 14 seconds meets it, even though his PRISMA-7 of 2 is below the threshold of 3.

whyNot.0: PRISMA-7 indicates frailty at 3 or more; his score is 2.
whyNot.1: A PRISMA-7 below 3 does not cancel a Timed Up and Go result that indicates frailty.
whyNot.3: NG56 lists both PRISMA-7 and Timed Up and Go for hospital outpatient settings.

B.q: Mrs Begum, 82, is admitted with pneumonia and today needs two staff to move in bed. Two weeks ago she washed and dressed herself but needed help with shopping, housework, all outside activities and bathing. Which Clinical Frailty Scale score should be recorded?
options: Level 7, based on her current dependence
Level 6, based on her usual state
Level 8, based on how unwell she is
Level 5, based on her personal care
B.why: The CFS is scored on the person's baseline, about two weeks before the acute illness. Help with all outside activities, housework and bathing while managing personal care is level 6.

whyNot.0: Her current dependence reflects the acute illness; scoring today inflates the CFS.
whyNot.2: Level 8 means dependent and approaching end of life; being acutely unwell is not the same.
whyNot.3: Level 5 needs help with higher-order tasks; she needed help with all outside activities and bathing, which is level 6.

B.q: During a long-term condition review, Mr Webb, 80, is asked to rate his health on a scale from 0 to 10. He answers 6. How does NICE NG56 interpret this?
options: It indicates frailty, as 6 or less is the threshold
It shows no frailty, as the threshold is 4 or less
It needs a Timed Up and Go result before it can be interpreted
It shows no frailty, as the threshold is 5 or less
B.why: NG56 recs 1.4.4–1.4.5: self-reported health status scores of 6 or less out of 10 indicate frailty.

whyNot.1: The NICE threshold is 6 or less, not 4 or less.
whyNot.2: Self-rated health is a stand-alone NG56 tool; a second test is not needed to interpret it.
whyNot.3: The threshold is 6 or less, so a score of 6 indicates frailty.

C.q: Mr Lewis, 86, has moderate dementia. His recent memory is very impaired, although he recalls events from his past well, and he manages his personal care with prompting. He is not acutely unwell. Which Clinical Frailty Scale level is the usual starting point for him?
options: Level 4, very mild frailty
Level 5, mild frailty
Level 6, moderate frailty
Level 7, severe frailty
C.why: The CFS guidance says the degree of frailty generally corresponds to the degree of dementia. Moderate dementia, with personal care possible with prompting, corresponds to moderate frailty, level 6.

whyNot.0: Very mild frailty does not match moderate dementia with very impaired recent memory.
whyNot.1: Mild frailty corresponds to mild dementia, such as forgetting details of a recent event.
whyNot.3: Severe frailty corresponds to severe dementia, where personal care is not possible without help.

C.q: A community nurse visiting Mrs Shah, 81, at home wants to use a NICE NG56 frailty tool listed for primary and community care. Mrs Shah is well today. Which tool fits that setting?
options: The Timed Up and Go test
The PRISMA-7 questionnaire
The Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly
The 4AT rapid assessment
C.why: NG56 rec 1.4.4 lists informal or formal gait speed, self-reported health status and the PRISMA-7 questionnaire for primary and community care.

whyNot.0: NG56 lists Timed Up and Go for hospital outpatient settings, not primary and community care.
whyNot.2: The Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly is listed for hospital outpatient settings.
whyNot.3: The 4AT assesses delirium and cognitive impairment, not frailty.

C.q: Mr Tan, 77, lives alone and does all his own personal care, shopping, cooking and finances. He says he feels 'slowed up' and tired during the day, and these symptoms now limit what he does. Which Clinical Frailty Scale level fits best?
options: Level 2, fit with no active disease symptoms
Level 5, living with mild frailty
Level 3, managing well
Level 4, living with very mild frailty
C.why: CFS v2.0 level 4 marks the early transition from complete independence: not dependent on others for daily help, but symptoms limit activities, often described as being 'slowed up' or tired.

whyNot.0: Level 2 describes someone with no active disease symptoms.
whyNot.1: Level 5 needs help with higher-order tasks such as finances or transport; he manages these.
whyNot.2: Level 3 has well-controlled problems without symptoms limiting activities; his symptoms now limit him.

reteach.title: Frailty is a story, not a snapshot
reteach.question: Why does a nurse ask the family how someone was two weeks ago, rather than scoring what she sees on the ward today?

blocks.h: The baseline tells you the reserve
blocks.body: Acute illness makes almost everyone look frail. The Clinical Frailty Scale is useful because it captures the person's usual level of function, which predicts how they will cope and what treatment will help. So the nurse asks: what could you do on your own two weeks ago? Finances and transport (level 5)? All outside activities and bathing (level 6)? Personal care (level 7)?

blocks.h: Climbing down the scale by what help is needed

blocks.text: No Timed Up and Go or gait speed test while the person is acutely unwell (NICE NG56 rec 1.4.3).

explain.body: CFS v2.0 runs from 1 Very fit to 9 Terminally ill. Levels 4 to 8 describe living with very mild, mild, moderate, severe and very severe frailty. The key is what help the person needs: higher-order tasks (5), all outside activities and bathing (6), personal care (7).

test.q: Which description matches Clinical Frailty Scale level 7?
options: Needs help with finances and heavy housework
Dependent for personal care, but stable
Dependent and approaching the end of life
Independent, but slowed up and tired
test.why: Level 7, living with severe frailty: completely dependent for personal care, yet stable and not at high risk of dying within about 6 months.

whyNot.0: Help with finances and heavy housework describes level 5.
whyNot.2: Dependence while approaching end of life describes level 8.
whyNot.3: Independent but slowed up describes level 4.

explain.body: Score the person's usual state about two weeks before the acute illness, using history from the person, family, carers and records, plus clinical judgement. In dementia, frailty generally corresponds to the degree of dementia.

test.q: On which period of the person's life is the Clinical Frailty Scale score based?
options: Their function on the day of admission
Their function on the day of discharge
Their usual state about 2 weeks before illness
Their best level of function at any point in the previous year
test.why: The CFS describes the person's baseline, about two weeks before the acute illness began.

whyNot.0: Function on admission reflects the acute illness and overstates frailty.
whyNot.1: Discharge function may still be affected by the admission.
whyNot.3: The best function in a year may be out of date; the reference is about two weeks before the illness.

explain.body: Primary and community care: informal or formal gait speed, self-reported health or PRISMA-7. Hospital outpatients: self-reported health, Timed Up and Go, formal gait speed, PRISMA-7 or the Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly. Thresholds: TUG over 12 s, gait over 5 s for 4 m, PRISMA-7 of 3 or more, self-rated health 6 or less.

test.q: In an outpatient clinic, which Timed Up and Go time indicates frailty under NICE NG56?
options: More than 8 seconds
More than 10 seconds
More than 15 seconds
More than 12 seconds
test.why: NG56 rec 1.4.5: a Timed Up and Go time of more than 12 seconds indicates frailty.

whyNot.0: 8 seconds is below the NICE threshold of 12 seconds.
whyNot.1: 10 seconds is below the NICE threshold of 12 seconds.
whyNot.2: 15 seconds is above frailty, but the threshold itself is more than 12 seconds.

explain.body: NICE says be cautious about assessing frailty in a person who is acutely unwell, and do not use a physical performance tool (such as gait speed or Timed Up and Go) at that time. Use history to score the baseline instead.

test.q: Mr Ward, 86, was admitted 6 hours ago with an exacerbation of heart failure and is breathless at rest. A colleague suggests doing a Timed Up and Go now to grade his frailty. What is the best response?
options: Do it now, so the score is ready for the ward round
Do it with a walking aid to reduce his effort
Defer it and gather his baseline from family
Replace it with a 4-metre gait speed test today
test.why: NG56 recs 1.4.2–1.4.3: be cautious about assessing frailty when someone is acutely unwell and do not use a physical performance tool. Gather his baseline history instead.

whyNot.0: Testing during an acute illness gives a misleading result and is not recommended.
whyNot.1: A walking aid does not change the advice: no performance tools while acutely unwell.
whyNot.3: Gait speed is also a physical performance tool, so it should not be used now either.
